text: "World War Zimmerman" is the third episode of the seventeenth season of the American animated television series South Park and the 240th episode of the series overall. It premiered on Comedy Central in the United States on October 9, 2013. The episode parodies the 2013 film World War Z and the killing of Trayvon Martin by George Zimmerman. Eric Cartman draws attention by acting unusually nice to Token Black and having nightmares while asleep in class. When his counselor, Mr. Mackey, questions him, Cartman claims Token is a "ticking time bomb." His nightmares depict him as Brad Pitt's character in World War Z, with African Americans, including Token, playing the zombies who riot after the Zimmerman trial verdict. With Mackey's encouragement, Cartman reads a poem to Token and later performs a musical version of it at a student assembly, disavowing any connection to the Zimmerman case. When Token takes offense at being portrayed as someone to feel bad for, Cartman, fearing the "outbreak has started," goes to his house for his survival kit, picks up a random woman, and commandeers a passenger plane at an airport, warning passengers they can only stop the end of the world by finding a place where the "contagion" cannot reach them. On the plane, Cartman discovers a black passenger in the bathroom and barricades him in. When the passenger tries to break out, the other passengers panic, leading to the plane crashing in the Rocky Mountains. Cartman and the woman survive and go to Jimbo's gun store to buy a rifle to kill Token, but Jimbo refuses to shoot anyone unless threatened in his own home. After considering this, Cartman and the woman head to Florida to shoot George Zimmerman to stop the outbreak. The woman is run over and killed. Cartman goes to the Zimmerman home wearing black paint on his face. Zimmerman shoots Cartman, which is praised by officials as having apparently saved them, but one agent discovers Cartman is white. Zimmerman is then tried, found guilty, and executed via electrocution for attempted murder. Cartman survives the shooting and returns to South Park, where he apologizes to Token, who is upset. Cartman then tricks Token into moving close enough to shoot him in accordance with the stand-your-ground law. At school, Cartman is sent to Mackey's office with a bandaged Token. When Mackey demands they apologize to resolve their "feud," Token angrily denounces the stand-your-ground law for not applying to black people. Cartman panics again and flees, causing another plane crash. The animation for Cartman's dream sequences was completed very early in the production cycle of the season, as series co-creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone developed the idea during the annual "writers retreat" between seasons sixteen and seventeen. They originally intended to expand on the dream sequence and use it for the season's premiere, with the episode consisting almost entirely of the dream sequence and revealing Cartman's awakening at the end. Parker was pleased they abandoned this idea because it is one of the very few episodes his father told him he did not understand, and he believed his father would have disliked it even more if they had stuck with the original concept, as he had not seen World War Z. Parker noted that the writers were pleased with the episode, stating that the season's third episode is typically when they "shaken off the rust." Token being shot at the end was originally intended to be a permanent death, inspired by a similar storyline in The Simpsons, but it was quickly changed because Parker and Stone "love having Token around." In its original American broadcast, "World War Zimmerman" was watched by 2.056 million overall households, according to Nielsen Media Research, and received a 1.2 rating/5 share among adults aged 18 to 49. Marcus Gilmer of The A.V. Club gave the episode an "A−," saying, "Some of those moments were brutal but it in a meaningful, impactful, and, yes, even funny way. That's what satire does when it works: It scorches." Max Nicholson of IGN rated the episode 8.7 out of 10, noting that "I always know it's a great episode of South Park when I have to walk on eggshells just to review it," and praised the "great social commentary," concluding it was "a return to form for South Park." Chris Longo of Den of Geek gave the episode four and a half stars out of five, describing it as featuring "classic Cartman" and concluding with "when South Park took an extended hiatus, we dreamed it would pay off in well-thought out, precisely executed performances like these. Bravo, Matt and Trey." Josh Kurp of Uproxx described being left "speechless" and compared Cartman's behavior in the episode to his actions in the fifth season episode "Scott Tenorman Must Die."
